To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the responsiveness of general practitioner (GP) practices to price was not greater for fundholders than for non-fundholders, that the price of the referral was not a primary consideration in their referral decisions and that, as a result of this, the potential for price competition to reduce the costs of elective care was not realized.
fundholding GPs in the city of Leicester did not respond to price in their referrals to competing hospitals, and this finding was not significantly different from non-fundholding GPs.
there is no evidence that fundholding general practices in the United Kingdom respond to price.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether healthcare markets work like other markets.
the extent to which budget-holding GPs responded to price during the fundholding era in the United Kingdom.
the responsiveness of general practitioner (GP) fundholders to prices in the UK's internal market.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
price is a secondary consideration in the referral decisions made by fundholders.

the evidence from our study does not provide a basis for the view that the introduction of GP fundholding in the United Kingdom was likely to result in significant savings from a more efficient use of resources.
the British experiment in GP fundholding has not provided evidence to support the view that price is a major factor in determining the behaviour of budget-holding physicians in the UK.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the market for healthcare is not a market for health.
the evidence from this study is consistent with the view that fundholding practices do not respond to the prices of procedures.
, in this particular case, fundholders did not respond to prices.
The main takeaway from our work is that
policymakers should avoid the temptation to assume that the actors in healthcare markets will respond to price, even when they have been given incentives to do so.
the responsiveness of budget-holding physicians to prices may be very limited.
, in the case of elective care, price is unlikely to have been a major factor in the behaviour of GPs in the fundholding scheme.
